title: Finding Most Influential Sets
claim: A greedy procedure that picks the most influential single item first can miss the jointly optimal set, whose influence is masked individually.
layout: 1 panel, scatter plot with three overlaid fit lines, legend by direct labels
description: A single 2-D scatter plot titled '3-MIS' with x from 0 to 4 and y from 0 to 3. Five points are shown. Two orange points at the lower left (x=0 and x=1) lie near an orange dashed line labeled 'Greedy', which has a shallow positive slope. One black point sits at x=2, y≈1.5. Two teal points sit at the top right (x=3 and x=4, y≈3.1). A solid teal horizontal line labeled 'Optimal' passes through the teal points, and 'A' labels the top-right region. A black dotted line labeled 'Full (β̂ = 0.84)' rises diagonally through the data. The contrast between teal, orange and black lines shows how the greedy and optimal fits diverge. The eye goes first to the flat teal line at the top, then to the diverging dashed and dotted lines.
caption: Greedy failure when finding the $3$-MIS for $n = 5.$ Point A is the most influential singleton and is therefore selected first by a greedy procedure. The exact $3$-MIS instead consists of the three leftmost points, whose influence is joint and masked in singleton rankings. Enumeration recovers the optimal leave-set-out slope of $0$ (solid teal line), while greedy selection is trapped on a suboptimal path.
abstract: Identifying most influential sets (MIS) - size-$k$ subsets whose removal maximally changes a target estimand - is typically infeasible because it requires searching over $\binom{n}{k}$ subsets. For estimands with linear-fractional leave-set-out effects, we show that MIS selection reduces to a one-parameter sequence of top-$k$ problems. Dinkelbach's method yields an algorithm with $\mathcal{O}(n)$ cost per iteration and finite termination. For fixed residualized inputs, the algorithm returns a globally optimal set for the univariate ratio objective, including the oracle-residualized partial linear model. With estimated nuisance functions, uniform denominator and generated-score stability imply approximation to the first-order oracle orthogonal-score objective; exact set recovery follows under a separation condition. Simulations and applications show that the method recovers exact MIS that were previously computationally inaccessible.
